Oral evidence - 17 Nov 2026

Built Environment Committee

Uncorrected oral evidence: Maintenance and enforcement in public spaces

Tuesday 17 November 2026

10.50 am

Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Gascoigne (The Chair); Baroness Andrews; Lord Bailey of Paddington; Lord Bassam of Brighton; Lord Cameron of Dillington; Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe; Baroness Janke; Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon; Lord Porter of Spalding; Lord Ravensdale.

Evidence Session No. 3 Heard in Public Questions 17 – 31

Witnesses

Rosie Apperley, Projects Coordinator, Octopus Community Network; Dr Joseph Owen, Senior Research Fellow, University of Southampton; Mark Webb, Managing Director, The Business Hive.

USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT

This is an uncorrected transcript of evidence taken in public and webcast on www.parliamentlive.tv.

Any public use of, or reference to, the contents should make clear that neither Members nor witnesses have had the opportunity to correct the record. If in doubt as to the propriety of using the transcript, please contact the Clerk of the Committee.

Members and witnesses are asked to send corrections to the Clerk of the Committee within 14 days of receipt.

Examination of witnesses

Rosie Apperley, Dr Joseph Owen and Mark Webb.

The Chair: Good morning and welcome to the House of Lords Built Environment Committee. Over the last few weeks, we have been looking into the enforcement and maintenance of the public realm. This is our third evidence session, and we are going to focus a bit more on the grass-roots and community organisations that are out there doing good work.

We have three witnesses before us. Dr Owen is a senior research fellow at the University of Southampton and, among other things, has done a lot of work around the role of culture and place-making. Rosie Apperley is the projects co-ordinator at Octopus Community Network, which is a series of centres around north London that focus on social support for different organisations there. Mark Webb is the managing director of The Business Hive, which supports grass-roots organisations and businesses in north Lincolnshire. Welcome to all three of you.

We have a series of questions to ask you. Please try to bring to life some of your answers with your own experiences, be it something that you have had direct experience of or something that you have found to be interesting. Give us as much evidence as you can, as well as solutions, not just around money but for some of the things you think could be fixed more easily. There may be questions that you do not feel you know the answer to or that someone else has answered. Do not feel like you need to fill the time. Your time is very precious, so we will try to keep our questions short. I am going to go straight into the first one. I want to get an understanding, in the crudest sense, as to why the maintenance of the public realm and public spaces matters. From your own experiences, what does a well-managed public space mean to a local area? I will start with you, Mark, and your experience up in Grimsby, please.

Mark Webb: Thank you. We are based in north-east Lincolnshire, just to clarify.

This is quite an interesting general question and the best way I can answer it is with this example. We all know the idea that one broken window leads to other broken windows, which leads to the degradation of buildings. Taking note of that is important not just because of the infrastructure but because of the impact it has on people. It applies to people. The community of Great Grimsby, for example, are well-beleaguered by everyone, with lots of people telling them how bad their town is. If they walk out into the high street and see a broken window—or if they see a public space or a green space that is uncatered for—how are they ever really going to believe in their own future, let alone the future of their town? It has a direct impact on them and how they feel.

It might be difficult to imagine how an empty, boarded-up shop could result in somebody not caring about their education, but for the young people who walk through the town and see that no one really cares about where they live, are they going to care about what happens in the classroom or to them in the future? It is important to draw that correlation.

The reverse is also true. I will give you an example. We have a public-private-led partnership called the 2025 Group. We recently put planters down on our high street because it looked a bit like somewhere from eastern Europe that had been left alone—there was concrete and not much else. The community were talking about wanting to make it look better and feel safer, so we put down planters; I am sure you have seen that before. The interesting thing was that one of the planters went round a pub. You would not think that day drinkers would be the normal type of people who would be the supporters of our area. However, I witnessed somebody walking past the pub, where day drinkers were sitting having their pints, and they put out a cigarette butt in one of the planters. The day drinkers all stood up and said, “Hey, you can get that out of there. That’s our planter”. They were defending what had been put in place at their pub. That is the immediate impact. If that is just one planter and a few day drinkers, imagine what difference it could make to the community as a whole. That is why I think it is important.

The Chair: Thank you very much. Rosie, could you elaborate from your experience? Also, are there examples you can give about where that is not being done or not being well maintained?

Rosie Apperley: Absolutely. To follow on from what Mark said about people feeling like their area is cared for, we want people to be active citizens in their community and society. If they do not feel that their area is cared for and that no one cares for them, we are never going to get there.

Islington is interesting. As I am sure many of you will know, there is vast inequality in the borough. There are parts of the borough that are very deprived and parts that are very affluent. For example, Nag’s Head town centre, which is where Holloway Road meets Seven Sisters Road, is quite a deprived part of the borough. There was a fire in a takeaway shop earlier this year or maybe late last year. The building was left for months, and because of where the building was, a street pedestrian crossing had to be closed for months. One of our community centres is based just around the corner, and people were coming in and saying, “The council don’t even care whether I can cross the road safely”. This was a crossing between a bus stop and a bank, and it was very heavily used.

With the area being generally quite run-down anyway and then feeling abandoned when something serious had happened, it led to people coming to their local community centre and saying, “No one cares. In other parts of the borough, which are just round the corner, this would not happen”. Whether that is true or not, that is their experience. They feel that if there were a fire in another part of the borough that is very affluent, it would be cleared up, and the pedestrian crossing would be back in use very quickly. Whereas they are just left in their generally quite run-down area because nobody cares about them.

The Chair: Thank you, Rosie. Dr Owen, over to you.

Dr Joseph Owen: I echo those points. People recognise a cared-for place—they see when a place is cared for. The only thing that I would add is that physical infrastructure—and making sure that it is maintained and looked after—is important. This is also about the social infrastructure and what these places represent. For a park, the park bench is important, but it is also about how that place is used. There is a link between physical infrastructure, whether it is benches, bins or whatever, and how that place is then used by the community. It is important to think about the social ties and the feelings of safety—the emotional attachments that Mark alluded to that are linked to the physical infrastructure. It is not just about tidying up a space. If you fix something and tidy it up, it does not necessarily create pride. What creates pride is people having agency over that to understand why it is happening and who has done it, and whether they have a role in doing it is important. There is not necessarily a causation between a really well-looked-after public space or realm and people feeling an attachment to it and having pride in it.

I have lots of evidence from lots of different projects that we have worked on, but I can speak as a resident in one instance. I am originally from Portsmouth and, during Covid, when I went back home, I emailed the parks directorate at Portsmouth City Council about a local park where I used to play when I was a kid. I said, “There’s a lovely view of Portsmouth from this park, but you can’t actually see it because there’s nowhere to sit right at the top of the hill, where the park undulates. Would it be possible to install some benches there? I think they would be used and have value”. I could only do that because I suddenly started working with local authorities; I had some agency. I realised that they were not opaque institutions and that you could ask them to do something and they might do it.

Anyway, I think there was a period of consultation and when I went back, it must have been at Christmas, I walked up to the park and there they were: the benches were installed. The feeling that I had when I saw that was quite incredible—a sense of “Wow. I did that” or “I contributed to that”. It is that sense of empowerment and possibility that develops attachments with public space and with the public realm. I saw kids hanging out canoodling on one bench and then on another bench someone who had been walking their dog and was taking a break. I thought, “Wow. That’s incredible”.

The one addendum to that is that a couple of weeks later I was alerted that on the local Facebook group—I am not on it, of course—it said that someone had graffitied on one of the benches. There was a bit of outcry on the Facebook group, with people saying, “What a shame. We don’t deserve nice things. We got this thing and then it was desecrated in some way”. But for me, I just thought that that was actually an illustration of it being used by the people who needed to use it—in this case, presumably, young people.

There will always be an ambivalence attached to how we use public space, but it is important to understand the connection between the social use of something and the way in which it is presented. There is perhaps a more complicated question there.

The Chair: On your point about agency and so on, from your academic background and your experiences across the country, would you say that that is something that is universally always recognised across the country? Is it something that is happening? Do you think that local authorities, for example, such as the one you mentioned, want and are willing to work on it?

Dr Joseph Owen: Absolutely—agency is one of those things that is almost universal in determining the success of something. No doubt we will talk about the Pride in Place boards as part of this work.

The Chair: I do not want to jump; that question is to come.

Dr Joseph Owen: Having agency is really important, and, importantly, that is different from having pride. Perhaps they overlap, but it is also important to be clear about the terms of reference that we are using in these conversations. Agency is one of the things that is measured in the Community Life Survey. It is important to think about how you might be able to scale some of those metrics for a high-profile area or a Pride in Place area—to be able to demonstrate change over a period of time and whether people feel that the intervention in the public realm has actually made them feel differently about their place or have a greater sense of agency over it. We have done lots of work in Southampton, which is where I am based institutionally, and we have seen that agency is really important. There are lots of tools and models with which to get there, but, again, that is for a later question.

Lord Bailey of Paddington: I am going to start with Rosie and then probably spread out from there. Do people want to take care of their areas? I am miserable about the middle classes taking over places that were built for working-class communities, and having it their way. But, in their defence, they are doing the work, so I am ambivalent; I should probably calm down on that. What evidence is there that people want to do it? In Rosie’s example, that was fine because it was done to the community, but in many examples—I have been a youth worker for over 35 years—it is the community that does not look after or abuses its surroundings. What evidence is there that people actually want to look after their situation?

In addition, who is responsible for spreading the notion of agency and how do we do it? Although I am miserable about the busybodies, they are busy, largely, trying to do the right thing. How can you spread that agency?

Rosie Apperley: On the question of whether people want to do it, we do a lot of work on housing estates in Islington, primarily around green space. Obviously, a lot of people on housing estates do not have private green space. Islington is very dense; it has the least green space per person of any borough in the country, I think. Where there is land, it is on estates. Recently, we have been doing a lot of work with residents who want to create a new green space on their estate that they feel they can actively use. We have been working to create it with them, helping them to have the skills to look after it, through workshops, and then handing it over to them. For us, the important thing is that people will be much more likely to want to look after a space if they have been involved in its design and in physically creating it, if they can. It is absolutely about having that agency.

Where there is difficulty is, first, where a space is created and people are told, “Right. You go and look after that”, and, secondly, where people do not feel that the council are doing the very basics. There will be a certain amount of looking after a space that has to be done by statutory services. That needs to be done so that residents feel that it is not just them and that it is a group effort. They might think, “We can look after our little bit on our estate, and we can grow veg and share it, but I want to know that my bins will be collected and that they’re not going to make a massive mess”.

To touch on the question of “who”, I will always say this: working with community organisations and locally trusted organisations such as community centres, which have often been around for decades, is vital. They have those trust relationships with people. I can maybe go into this a bit more later, but it is a model we are looking at, particularly in looking after green space, where there is what we are calling a local nature anchor. One of our community centres is taking the lead in its immediate geographic area to, where possible, do some maintenance itself through SLAs. It is about going to a local organisation, not a big corporate—a place where, on the simplest level, there is a tool store where a resident can come and borrow a litter pick or a shovel because they do not have one themself. It can be a hub for knowledge and resources. We can build that agency through the organisations that already exist and are trusted.

Mark Webb: It is a really interesting question; you are frustrated at the middle class and how that all works. A really divisive thing happens in our communities when people say, “Look at them, typical middle class. They’ve got agency, as does the council, and the people who are affected haven’t”. When it comes down to it, you cannot do for your community without your community. You cannot do things for them unless you involve them right from the beginning. I will give you an example.

The Business Hive works on enterprise, which we think is a great leveller for people who want to go into self-employment and whatnot. By way of example of how this can work, we took over a building that had an old empty social club attached to it. We did it up and offered it out for lease to somebody to run the social club, right in the heart of quite a deprived estate. As we were trying to offer it out, it was getting damaged—it was being vandalised, windows were broken practically every week, there was spray paint, et cetera. Then a lady from the estate came. We talked to her and took her through how to set up the business, and she was very keen. Obviously, she had noticed that it was being vandalised. When she signed the lease and took it on, she said, “I’ll sort out this mess”. She knew who was responsible and she went round to the people on the estate and said, “That is my place now. You leave it alone. I know where your mum and dad are. I’ll be telling them if you do that again”, and it stopped overnight, instantaneously. The community got involved and started planting.

The point here is that we can have all the security and council funding that we want but, in the end, you have to involve the community in the idea of what you are trying to create, right from the beginning—not when you have the money. Then you will get buy-in. It will take a long time, and you have to prove it; you have to show it. Everyone plays their part: the people who are receiving it, the middle class who is trying to shout loud about it, the council who is trying to enable it and the Government who are trying to fund it. Stop trying to divide them; they should all be going for one thing, and that is whatever the community wants to have in its place.

Baroness Andrews: Thank you; that was really interesting. I have a specific question for Rosie and then one very short one for everyone. Rosie, what inspired the creation of Octopus? Was it a sense that something had to be done that was not being done by any of the statutory agencies or any of the people who were technically responsible in the community?

My second question is for Mark. You mentioned people telling other people what a horrible place they live in—how would you feel better about that? Is there some metric—maybe Joseph is doing this sort of work—that actually tells us this? We have not had any hard evidence, really, that things have got worse over the past decade. Are things worse, basically? That is a simple question, and I ask for a short answer.

Rosie, what is the story of Octopus?

Rosie Apperley: I will start with Octopus, but I will also tell you about the community centres, because that speaks a little more to that. Octopus was founded in 1999, when there was a round of austerity cuts that were going to hit all the community centres. They had previously been 100% grant funded by the local authority, and that was going to stop. My colleague Julie, who was one of the founding members, was a business adviser at the time and felt that, rather than each of the community centres trying to figure out how on earth effectively to become small businesses by themselves, they should come together. They employed a firefighter fundraiser and then had a fundraiser and, within a couple of years, had got nearly £1 million to run a healthy living initiative programme. I guess the challenge there was that lots of people were working separately and they needed to bring them together to survive.

A lot of the community centres in our network have come out of social action by residents. One example is Hanley Crouch, which has a new building now but it was based in an old laundry. That building had closed, was not being used and was empty. A group of local mothers did not have anywhere to take their toddlers to socialise, so they took over the building. That has then become a community centre that has existed for 40 years. A lot of the centres have a similar story, where residents have felt something was missing and have created it. That speaks to their agency. I do not know, but maybe we do not do things like that as much any more. Across the network, we are really proud of the feeling that we can see that there is a gap and take over a space, and then, decades later, it is still supporting families.

Baroness Andrews: That means that you have been picking up bits of central government grants rather than local government grants for healthy living neighbourhood stuff, city challenge, and God knows what else—there have been so many. So that has been the model—that is very interesting. What about the question of whether it is getting worse?

Dr Joseph Owen: Expectations change. Perhaps things are not getting worse on some metrics, but what people expect from their place shifts. The public realm is an ever-evolving thing, and people’s perception of it is always shifting as well. A good example is Southampton, where we have worked a lot. There are a few ward areas—small hyperlocal areas, or perhaps neighbourhoods—that that are predicated on a garden city vibe. They have lots of lovely green space. Mansbridge in Southampton, for instance, was designed just over 100 years ago, and there was a celebratory event about the architect Herbert Collins, who designed it. There was a bringing together of the community there. There is lots of green space and, as Rosie was saying, green space is one of those markers of pride and attachment. That is almost universal, and plenty of reports illustrate that.

However, obviously what has happened in the 100 years since is that we have mass car ownership, and places such as Mansbridge, for instance, are completely overwhelmed by the number of cars in the area, which then park on the green spaces because there is nowhere else to go. That is a great example of how something that is perfectly well designed, and could be looked after, becomes unfit for purpose in some ways, insofar as the expectations of what people need to do in that space change.

On agency and answering that question around what evidence there is about whether people care in their community, there is a paternalistic element to the idea of this figure who built this garden city space that is beautiful in its own right, but people do not necessarily now have that sense of attachment to or ownership of that. It is about how you can shape those places with respect for that history while also trying to adapt the place for the ways that people actually use that space now. Again, that goes back to the social infrastructure as much as it does to the physical infrastructure.

Mark Webb: I will answer that question about whether things have got worse. I genuinely do not think they have got worse. It is our perception, because of things such as social media, where everyone piles in about how bad everything is. The silent majority in Great Grimsby want—or will or hope—everything about their community spaces to happen.

For example, in partnership with Our Future we set up something called the 2025 Group, which was basically a group of businesspeople who said, “We just want to talk about the good stuff. We want to encourage the silent majority, who do not dare go on Facebook and say, ‘Actually, I’m quite enjoying life here’”. We started to fill town halls, talking about the good stuff that was happening, and that brought ideas from people in the community, who said, “What about this?” and, “Can that happen?”

I do not think it has got worse; I just think that we are slow to catch up with the changes in society and the way that society works. That is echoed on the high street, where we had a massive dependence on retail but no longer have. We are slow to get that round, and it is the same with the rest of the community. We just have to speed up, which means giving agency to everyone in the community and giving them a voice that is not on Facebook or any other platforms that are available.

The Chair: On the subject of speeding up, we are still stuck on the first question. Baroness Janke, I think you wanted to ask something.

Baroness Janke: We mentioned the idea of busybodies, and I was very interested in how Mark answered on that. I have similar examples in my own area in south Bristol, which is not considered the posh area of the city at all. There was a park there, and a group—I think it was mainly of parents—took charge of it. They wanted the park to be kept nice, with a nice piece of green space and places they could visit. There were a lot of young boys in the area that were using it for football and vandalising the plants and the things that they put there. As you said about your example, the parents got together and found another place where they could play football. They insisted on maintaining the green space for older people: mums with children and prams, and so on. That was how they took control, but at the start I am sure they were seen as busybodies who had overreached themselves.

My question is: how do you overcome this, where you have volunteers who are not the council and do not necessarily have the power to enforce things? They put work in and take ownership of a project, and they do not want to see it vandalised and used for other reasons—populated by drug dealers or whatever. How do you find the interface between the authorities who have the power to enforce action and the volunteers who rely on good will or their standing in the community?

Mark Webb: First, we should not presume that because people are in the community or from working class backgrounds, they do not have a voice. I know some very powerful people in the community who have very loud voices and they get things done—that is for sure.

I will give you an example in answer to your question. A few years ago, when CCGs were in the health service, we had a group of volunteers called the Cancer Collaborative. They were people from some of the most deprived communities that had been affected so much by cancer. These people got together either because they had suffered from it or because their partners were affected by it. They were volunteers, and they did more to spread the message about what you should or should not do to prevent yourself falling ill with that dreadful disease, among some of the most deprived communities. I think someone offered to pay them once, which is a big mistake—that should never happen. All they needed was to be seen, valued and enabled by people such as the local authority and by any other body, and to be told, “What you are doing is important and impactful”. Do not give them forms to fill out but just support them; every now and then, give them a lunch somewhere to celebrate them. That is not being patronising but being very real. They loved the work that they did and it made a difference. So we should not assume that we have to put something in place; we should just find who they are and turn the volume up for their voices—make sure that they are amplified and give them the value.

Baroness Janke: They are the people who can feel they do not have the authority to stop the space being damaged or being used for other purposes.

Mark Webb: Then bring in people who feel that they have got the authority and connect them. Bring other people in the community together, whether they are middle class or working class, or whatever; bring them together and say, “This is important”.

Baroness Janke: What about the statutory agencies such as the local police, the council and so on?

Mark Webb: They should be enablers. In the local authority, the police and the fire services there should be people who enable it to happen. So much of the time those agencies get in the way, for good reasons, rather than trying to clear a path for those vociferous volunteers to make a difference. That is what they should do.

The Chair: I am sorry to interrupt but I am conscious that that is an area we will cover in quite a lot of detail later.

Lord Bassam of Brighton: I was a councillor back in 1983 in Brighton—I did it for 19 years or something.

Lord Bailey of Paddington: You need to make a declaration.

Lord Bassam of Brighton: I am not sure I need to declare being a councillor, but I was coming to my declaration. Thank you. I should add that I am also a director of place at Business in the Community, which has some bearing on this. The point I wanted to get to was: do you think there is a sort of sweet spot between public engagement through “friends of” groups, or groups that take some sort of ownership of a space which is publicly maintained, and making sure that local authority services are effective and perceived to be so by those groups? Can we use and mobilise the public to help perfect and improve the quality of maintenance in public spaces in particular? It seemed to me from my councillor experience that the thing that we were missing back in the 1980s was that degree of public engagement and that it was the impact of budgets becoming tighter—austerity, and so on—that forced many authorities, probably including my own later on, to fall back on public-spiritedness to fill the space that the local authority was not able to fund any more.

The Chair: Before anyone answers, it is a good prelude, Lord Bassam, but I will bring in Baroness Lawrence, because I think some of the questions she wants to focus on are also around how to make best use of money and resources. Do you want to start as well?

Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon: I do. Before I start, one of the things that Mark spoke about—please excuse my voice—was that woman who took over a space, and who knew the family and the boys and so on. That just reminded me of something that used to happen in the Caribbean, especially with teachers. If a child was doing something out of school, that teacher could say, “I will speak to your parents about this”. That sense of community is what needs to happen a lot more. In that way, a child would know what they are allowed to get away with, because they know that at some point the parents will hear what they are doing. I thought that was quite a good example.

My question is: over the years, the Government have awarded funding for communities to create and maintain public spaces. To what extent have these programmes been successful, and how could current or future funding streams be improved?

Dr Joseph Owen: I can speak to that last question. Have they worked so far? They have not in a way that has created positive, sustained change. We followed the towns fund originally and we did a survey of all 100 boards, which were fairly unrepresentative of the places that they were supposed to represent. The majority of decision-makers were white and over 50, and that is just going to cause a kind of narrow purview for understanding your place and being able to intervene usefully in it.

For the levelling up fund, there was obviously a big focus on glass and steel and not on the organisations and individuals who might be able to sustain those spaces and make them meaningful to the community.

Coming to Pride in Place, there is a bit of a shift there, but still 67%, I think, or 63% of it is capital funding rather than revenue, so again it should be about giving flexibilities to places and communities to decide how they want to spend the money. That is the important thing. It is not necessarily about more funding but about giving them the flexibility to deliver the programmes that they want to, which might be more towards the activities and individuals and organisations that already exist in those places—the capacity that is already there and which does the wider capacity building in those communities. So it is about identifying those. I hope that those boards across the UK are starting to do that. So we have seen a shift, but the competitive funding models, particularly under levelling up—

Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon: What advice would you give to those funders to shift and move things forward? At the end of the day, the community that is in those spaces is the community you are trying to make things better for. What advice would you give to the funders to bring in the community and help to make the space a lot better for them?

Dr Joseph Owen: There are three things. Give communities the flexibility to decide between the capital and revenue balance in terms of what they spend their money on. Give them proper support to co-design—that is the key thing that we always base our work on, having that really inbuilt co-design capacity from the start. There is also the measurement question: the ability to measure whether something has worked. That is what we are really keen to do with the Pride in Place neighbourhood boards. We have put in a funding bid that I hope will monitor and evaluate some of the work that the Pride in Place boards are doing. It is a 10-year programme, so there is an opportunity here to establish some baselines in year one and to be able to demonstrate that people have more agency over their community. That is something we can measure over time, but we need to put that kind of infrastructure in place now in order to be able to decide. So, again, it is about flexibility, support and co-design, and measurement of agency and things that matter to those communities.

Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon: Rosie, would you agree?

Rosie Apperley: I cannot speak directly in terms of our experience with things like Pride in Place—Islington is not a Pride in Place area. But generally, the message for me will always be that you have to involve people right at the beginning, not when things have already been designed in any way, and go through those trusted relationships with community organisations. Do not come in and try to find a way to engage people. These organisations do it day in, day out—they are on the ground, knocking on doors—so engage with those organisations that exist.

Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon: You are not imposing it on the community.

Rosie Apperley: No. It is also so much easier. I work a step removed from the centres, but if I say to one of the centres, “Can I come and talk to a group about X, Y and Z?”, half of that trust is already built because their community centre manager is inviting me in because they trust me, so you are five steps ahead already. So often we see things coming in externally, and maybe we are asked to get a few people in the room, but we have not been involved in what that is, and those trust relationships are so valuable to the centres that they cannot risk them. Unless they are involved from the beginning and they have that investment and ownership over the process, they will not risk the trust relationships they have with their communities because someone else wants them to.

Mark Webb: I would like to come back to Pride in Place and some incredible work that is going on in Great Grimsby with that—it is really different with Our Future. I would like to answer that question directly. On funding, I am not part of that in the private sector; it was relatively new to me 20 years ago or so. However, it seems always to have followed a pattern that somebody comes up with some funding idea, the council or somebody is invited to bid for that funding and are told, “These are the metrics we’re going to measure you by” and everyone writes a bid, then someone gets the money and it goes in place and then runs out. It was great at the time.

The bit that we have found, particularly with Pride in Place, which seems to ring true, is that before you even mention money and before you even start to think about it, step back and engage the community on what is actually needed. Have honest conversations about what is possible and what is not—do not kid people that they can have everything. Bring them into the conversation. When you realise what they want, then go out and say, “Right, we can fund a certain amount of this. From what you’ve said, these are the things that we are going to measure it on”. It has to be measured because it is public money—I get that—but start way back before you mention money. As soon as you bring in money, everyone starts asking how they are going to spend the money, rather than asking what they need. That is a big mistake that seems to have happened regularly.

Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon: That funding is only for a short period of time as well—it is not extended. Before you actually complete the work in the community, the funds run out and you are right back at the beginning again. How do we manage to talk to the authority giving out the funding and say that it is not a quick fix—it is something that it needs to keep investing in over a period of time, over two or three years? How do you suggest we do that?

Mark Webb: Ten years is really your bottom line—your minimum for some of the big, impactful, sustainable changes that you need to make, and which goes beyond electoral cycles. The secret to that is to make sure that you engage from the beginning people who are not being elected every five years. I know that they are civil servants, but they are also members of the community and community groups like Rosie’s. It is about getting them involved from the beginning, so that they have the momentum to take it forward. It does not matter what your politics are—it is part of what the community is doing, not what politicians are doing.

Baroness Andrews: On Pride in Place, I do not know whether any of you remember New Deal for Communities in the early 2000s, which was an almost identical model. It took place over 10 years, making sure that local people were fully engaged. It involved getting the matriarchs from the community to run the place, along with the local vicar. You would start not with the hanging baskets but with getting rid of the crack houses—because you would know where they are. I do not know what you think about this, Joseph. Was that scheme, which was so successful in part, properly evaluated? Is there something that we can learn from it specifically?

Moving on to Pride of Place, you said that it has most of the successful elements in place—the 10 years, and the fact that it is basically rooted in community knowledge and experience. I think that is what you are saying, but maybe not. What else does it need to make it a success? Are there things happening in Grimsby or other parts of the country? We had only 39 targeted areas in 2000 for the new deal—this involves 284. Will they be of a critical size to deliver change that is transferable, even outside their boundaries, in their local area?

That is one question. Sorry, this is a bit scattergun. Can I start with Joseph? On metrics and evaluation, does it stand a better chance of knowing what success looks like this time?

Dr Joseph Owen: Yes, if we get in early enough to be able to do it. The capacity is not really there at the moment. That is why, as researchers, there is a need for us to come in and do this work.

Baroness Andrews: Let me just pin that down. Where would the capacity have to be put, and who would have to fund it, in order to know at the end of the decade whether it had worked?

Dr Joseph Owen: Initially, it would have had to have been part earmarked within that Pride of Place funding. But there is still scope as researchers; we are working much more hand in glove with governmental organisations.

Baroness Andrews: There is no evaluation budget yet, is there?

Dr Joseph Owen: Not to my knowledge, but I do not know—I would have to check that. It is good to pick out the New Deal for Communities; that is something that we should look at. It is a bit before my time, but I will have a look at it.

There is an opportunity here for some degree of success with the Pride of Place neighbourhood boards, but it really depends on how these boards have been set up. Because of some of the short timescales in the setting-up periods for these boards, decisions have had to be made in different places whether to codesign the board or to have a genuinely consultative process for designing the board, or to focus on codesigning the plan at a later date. We can see the challenges of that trade-off already, if the board is predetermined, which will influence what the later decisions will be.

Baroness Andrews: Sorry, I am going to come back to you on that. Are all the boards set up, or are some of them being retrofitted?

Dr Joseph Owen: I do not know. Lots of them are set up by this point—I would assume that almost all of them are set up. There was a recent ICON report that has covered quite a lot of that initial process.

Baroness Andrews: So we need to fill in some of our own gaps. Mark, what do you think? What can we learn from you?

Mark Webb: Before Pride in Place came around, we had a local authority that worked with an organisation called Our Future. We started talking with the community—and by “the community” I mean every aspect of it, from businesses, the middle class and the working class, organisations, the public sector and everybody else. They were brought together not to talk about how we can spend money, as I referred to before, but to ask what the area needs. That was before Pride in Place funding was talked about—so we were already having this groundswell and starting to build up pride in what the area could be. That was quite important. Then Pride in Place funding came along, and that really fired up the conversation more. People were already engaged and already had agency, because we were starting by asking what we needed to do rather than what we needed to spend money on.

How that has unfolded with Pride in Place is that we are already ahead of the game in understanding what parts of our area needed attention, whether that was about thriving high streets, housing, health or education. Whatever it was that was required, we already had a start on it—and there were groups of interested people from every sector of the community involved in those discussions. The remarkable thing is that that kind of democratic involvement and engagement usually falls apart when it comes to the money, because suddenly somebody in Whitehall or in one of the councils asks what it is going to be spent on.

Pride in Place in Grimsby, which you can see on Grimsby Together, if you look online, has created decision-makers from people in the community. It has invited people from the community in to say, “We’ll help you, and the money will be spent on what you think is needed”. It is about direct influence. Those people will sit in a room a bit like this one, supported by organisations such as the Key Fund and Our Future. They will look at what has been put forward by other members of the community, who may be people living down street, and they will decide—as a group—what the community needs and what should be put forward. There are no councillors, big businesses or large communities involved—it is just people. Every stage of the funding is being decided in that way.

Obviously, it has to go through checks and balances to make sure that it is legitimate and feasible—all those things are done—but it starts with people in the community making those decisions. That has not been a government-directed or even a council-directed thing. It is because, together with Our Future, we have worked to enable it to happen in our town—and now people are going into chambers such as this one, people who have never been into a chamber, to make decisions about thousands of pounds of money for their community. Imagine if that happened right across the country—it would be remarkable.

Baroness Andrews: I have one final small question. It is going to be your decision, and you are going to be in charge of it. With the decent environment and the things that we are concerned about in this committee, how are they going to surface in these priorities? Will they be top of the list or halfway down the list?

Mark Webb: No, because one of the groups that we had was about the built environment and the environment. The discussions about what the town needs already had that as part of the playbook, on equal footing with town centres. Ultimately, we can decide that we want green spaces—but if the community at large wants something, that is where we start.

Lord Porter of Spalding: In referring to “They should sort this out”, who is “they”? Generally, “they” is central government, who subcontracts to local government. I am assuming that, at some point, the one holding the purse strings will be local government. North East Lincs ain’t the best example of political stability. Where you have allowed people to ask for whatever they want, regardless of whether it can be funded, I suggest that you have probably built up hope in people that has then not materialised, and they have then outed their local politicians as a consequence of that.

Mark Webb: That is a fair challenge.

Lord Porter of Spalding: I love Grimsby, and I recommend to anybody who has never had fish and chips in Grimsby to get up there and buy fish and chips, because it is fantastic. Do not all go to the smallest pub in the country at the same time—especially not if I want to drink in there—because you can only get two people at the bar. But it is a very nice shed on the railway.

When I first got engaged with Grimsby politically—it is in the same county as mine, even though it is further away from where I live than London is—it used to have a really good Labour administration, with people who really cared about the place they were in. Then we took it away from them as the blue team, because they did not deliver the things that they said. Then the blue team had it taken away from them by somebody else. I think that UKIP—not UKIP, Reform—has it now. Building up unmet expectation in the community is a dangerous space for a politician to be in. How do you get the community to own for themselves the final decision, rather than shunting it back to the politicians for not delivering the final vision?

Mark Webb: May I answer that? First of all, I thank you for that. I cannot tell you how much this is not a political thing. If, as a politician or as anyone, you stand up to the community and make them promises—

Lord Porter of Spalding: Everything in life is a political decision.

Mark Webb: Just let me finish that part. It is not about who the politicians are, what colour, stream or type of party they are in. Whoever you are, if you stand up in front of a group of community members and promise them something that you cannot deliver but say that you can, you are never going to gain their trust. That is why, if you start way before then—without the politicians in the room, necessarily—you can talk to them about what is and is not possible and what constraints you have. People are not stupid and they will understand the level of restraint that you are under, if you have that honest conversation. I am afraid that I am evidence of the fact that that is true.

Lord Porter of Spalding: It is the reverse of that evidence. I have just told you how politically unstable that place is.

Mark Webb: That is obviously an opinion that you hold; I do not agree with it. However, in the end, the changes in colour of local government have not impacted the development and the growth that we have been trying to work through, over the last five years. We do not work at that level. Of course, everything is politics, but politics comes and goes and works in five-year cycles If you have community organisers and people who love the place, you can work entirely on what is right for the community.

The stuff that that the Business Hive built as a social enterprise was regardless of the three different colours of local politics. I can honestly say that whoever goes into local politics goes into it because they want to help the community. If they do not, they have no business being there. That is the stance that I take. We will just get on with it and do it anyway.

The Chair: That is a good warm-up for the next area of questioning, which Baroness Griffin will lead on. I think you have some questions on this as well, so maybe you can jump ahead.

Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe: Yes, I do. I must apologise, because I have a medical appointment and will have to leave early. Can I just thank you? As somebody who had the privilege of representing the poorest ward in Liverpool, much of what you are saying resonates with me. Also, Mark, I agree that it should be the local community and not the councillors, although they have a role to play.

I want to ask you about measurement. In the UK, in the chain of production, we tend to do the product bit or the project bit, but we do not fund the R&D or the monitoring, evaluation and dissemination. We just do not do it. I loved what you said about the difference between pride and people having agency, but one of you mentioned that agency is actually being measured. There is a paradigm. What can we do about getting this right in the long term?

Dr Joseph Owen: I will come back on that. I will just give a quick historical illustration from a couple of years ago, with the levelling up fund. In the levelling up White Paper, one of the missions was to restore pride in place. That is when that language started to become quite prevalent in policy. We were working with local councils trying to write their bids, trying to do the monitoring and evaluation for that, and they were saying, “Well, we want to boost city pride” or “We want to restore pride”. Obviously, they had no metrics or baselines to work with. They had a kind of bricolage of previous consultations that they might be able to put together to constitute something that looked like something they could measure and could demonstrate change with.

Our initial worry was that you are really going to struggle to measure pride, given how complex and place-specific it is. Since then, however, we have thought more about using that Community Life Survey that I mentioned earlier—it is obviously a national survey—and scaling that to a neighbourhood level or to a Pride in Place area, basically asking the community what matters to them and what is meaningful for them. That is a qualitative response that you can elicit on their lived and felt experience. We have talked about this quite a bit already. From there, we would be able to map those to those existing indicators in order to do that comparison and measurement work.

That is the idea. It is never going to be perfect, but I feel that there is much more potential in a model whereby you ask people what is important for them and then have a bucket of metrics that you can map on to and demonstrate change with.

Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe: If you could give us examples in writing, I would be very grateful. Rosie, you were nodding.

Rosie Apperley: I am nodding, more from the perspective of a very small community organisation—we spoke about this briefly earlier—having researchers who could figure all this stuff out. How best do we measure these kinds of programmes and share them with local authorities and with small community organisations? You are right: we exist from grant fund to grant fund and there often is not time for research. A lot of grant funders now want you to take a community organising approach, but also want you to know what you are going to deliver when you write an application, which is not possible. It would be massively helpful to tiny organisations such as ours to have the time to do that listening with communities, which is the most important thing, and then also to have the people with the research background who can create these models that we can all pick up, use and measure, and then all be talking the same language.

Mark Webb: Very quickly, I think that, in this data-led world, we have a real opportunity to pull all the data that we pick up from areas and all the different organisations looking at and doing R&D. We should grab that information and pull it into one place that everyone can then use.

In terms of the indicators, the mistake that we make a lot of the time with funding is to ask for these measures at the beginning before you bid for it. What you should be saying is, “What do you need, how are you going to measure it so that it is robust at the end, and what is it going to look like?” We should not inflict measurements and metrics on a fund. Let them say, “This is how we are going to show you”, and that should be a part of the bid.

Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe: Thank you; I find this really useful. I am sorry; someone else will have to take my next question.

The Chair: That is absolutely fine. I think that the question that Baroness Griffin was going to get into was about—oh, sorry, Lord Ravensdale, do you want to jump in? Are you volunteering your services?

Lord Ravensdale: Thank you, Chair. I had a question to ask around some of this. We have talked about the evolution, I suppose, of the different models that have been used. We have talked about the levelling up funds, competitive bids and the shortfalls in that. We have now moved to Pride in Place, which addresses some of those issues in having longer-term funding not through competitive bids but through allocated areas. However, we have still highlighted some of the shortfalls there in terms of "We have all this money; how do we spend it?”—to think back to Mark’s contribution. Maybe that is not the right way round. I am interested in any thoughts on how we move to a model that is more locally led. We always have this issue that local areas have limited revenue-raising powers. However, we all agree that we want all this stuff to be locally driven.

Mark, maybe you could start us off. You talked about a model that you have got going in in Grimsby, which works pretty well. We have these great examples of models, but the question is always how to roll them out more broadly. How do we take examples of best practice and roll those out more broadly across the country? Do you have any thoughts on that, around the model itself and how we can evolve what is happening at the moment, so that it works better for local areas?

Mark Webb: My first answer would be that you cannot start here; you have to start some way back. In my view, if you wanted to create a model, you would go out to every area in the country and say, “What is it that you want? Build us a plan. We will give you a year; we will give you 18 months. We are not talking about money at the moment. What is it that this area really needs?” Grimsby will be very different to Spalding or very different to anywhere else. Find out what they want; talk about their areas of pressure and things that they need to create by engaging with the community in the way that I mentioned we had done with Our Future. Do that first.

Then submit a plan to the Government or the funders to say, “This is what this area needs, and we think this is how much it is going to cost”. Then it is a case of just working through it and making it a plan until the funders agree that plan, that they will fund this much of it and what outcomes they expect. Then every plan is individual, researched and thought about, and the community who wrote it, not the council, own it. On Lord Porter of Spalding’s point, it belongs to the community then, not to a political party. That is what I would say.

Lord Ravensdale: That is a good way of making it more locally driven. Rosie, can I have your thoughts from what you have seen? You mentioned Islington—not a not a Pride in Place area—which highlights one of the issues with the whole approach. What are your thoughts?

Rosie Apperley: I agree. Starting with listening is so important. I mentioned at the beginning that we take a community-organising approach and the start of that is always just to go out and listen. We were involved in a four-nation project called Nature Neighbourhoods, which was led by the National Trust, RSPB and WWF. We were a bit taken aback when we were asked to be involved because they picked 18 community partners from across the four nations and the request to us was: “Make a neighbourhood plan”. We are very used to being told that, if you are going to get money, you have to deliver X, Y, and Z in very specific ways.

The project worked really well. We spent 18 months going out, talking and listening to communities to explore what nature they wanted in their neighbourhood, and we now have a plan that we are delivering in collaboration with Islington Council and the National Trust.

In terms of your question about sharing knowledge, there have to be mechanisms where local governments can share good practice among themselves. Often in local government we find that it can be down to whether an individual is into an idea as to how well it works or whether they feel it is important to have involvement from the voluntary sector. Those individuals can obviously be completely different in different places. Then having need a mechanism by which other local authorities can pick up and take examples of good practice, rather than having to invent the how and the processes, would make a big difference.

Lord Ravensdale: Joseph, what are your thoughts on the overall model and how that could be evolved?

Dr Joseph Owen: You have given me an idea, actually. A colleague at Southampton has been working in Millbrook, which is a Pride in Place area, and has developed the NxtGen community research programme. That is about training residents to be community researchers, working in the place and understanding the needs of their fellow residents. It is about building people’s ability to influence and do that kind of work.

Just to jump ahead to think about how you scale that—because obviously these are all funded projects which are fairly targeted in places and need resource—I am currently seconded at the Local Government Association to do some work, and I think that would be a useful means to disseminate toolkits and resources. Although, yes, it is hard to say that we will fund a community research programme in each of these places, there are definitely resources or outputs that could be shared through the Local Government Association, for example. I think what is happening now, at least in universities, is that we are working so much more closely with organisations such as the LGA, as well as the councils, in order to have a wider reach with some of these models that we test.

Baroness Andrews: I have a question that Rosie is probably best placed to answer. A lot of this depends on the capacity of the voluntary or third sector, and usually funding for the third sector comes with the idea of “We would like you to deliver and we would like you to involve the community”. Are there any quick wins to be had in the context of building the capacity of the third sector and building social capital? We are talking about building social capital across all these programmes; is there anything we have missed or anything we should be prioritising in directing funding? For example, can we use any of the scope now developing for NEETs to hardwire apprenticeships and support staff, which will also enable young people to gain these important skills of decision-making and team-building? It is all about building capacity. That is just one personal obsession I have at the moment, but what do you think?

Rosie Apperley: Thanks for highlighting it, because the voluntary sector is struggling generally with capacity. I think part of it is a change of attitude, especially from local government. We are finding sometimes that it feels like local government is trying to keep more in-house because it feels like it could deliver. But if you are knocking on doors and trying to engage people on a council estate, it is different if you are a local community organisation to effectively being the landlord. So there is that kind of shift to trusting our voluntary sector partners to make decisions with us and going out and doing the work and be paid for it, rather than keeping stuff internally.

On the greening side, in particular, I mentioned earlier that we are exploring with Islington Council the potential for community organisations to agree service-level agreements to maintain certain areas, rather than paying big corporates who have no real connection with the borough but just get a contract. For example, one of our community centres has just taken on an SLA for a local community orchard. They will not just be arriving in the dead of night and watering; it will include volunteers and get the community involved. But the centre is being paid to do it rather than a big corporate organisation.

Baroness Andrews: That is a great innovation. It should be standard practice, should it not?

Lord Cameron of Dillington: I come from rural England, as it were, so market towns are what interests me. I am very taken by Mark’s concept that it is not the actual quality of the environment that gives people the quality of their lives; it is being involved in making it a quality environment that really makes all the difference. There are one or two run-down market towns where English Heritage or Historic England, or whatever it is called, has invested in the ancient buildings in the old town which has totally transformed those towns. It has made them attractive places for businesses to come to and people to build in. People from villages in what can be a 15-mile radius are coming to shop and use them as proper market towns. It is a different route, and I was wondering whether you could comment on the transformation that that sort of investment gives, as opposed to the people themselves doing it from the bottom up.

Mark Webb: We have been speaking a lot about people but it is really important to recognise that the same broken window analogy works in reverse; if you fix that window, then other ones do not get broken. Great Grimsby is probably not an example of a market town—however, I recognise that it happens in places such as Louth and Market Rasen near to us—but you have to have the courage to be able to recognise that what was once on your high streets and in those areas is no longer. Again, the idea of enabling comes. Town centres used to be a place where everyone gathered for everything, not just shopping, and it is just going back to that. It was only in the 1980s that that really happened. It is enabling that to happen. While you do not make decisions about opening up buildings and allowing community groups to come in and use those buildings to attract other people, the vacuum gets filled with vape shops, gambling shops and the like—not what the community asked for.

I am starting to sound like a stuck record, but you have to get behind the community saying, “We would like to see this in our town centre or our market town”, and then go out and enable that to happen. There are ways and means of doing it, such as pop-up shops, rate relief, wraparound business support and entrepreneurs. There are a whole lot of things waiting to make it happen, and one begets another. I have seen it in our town: you open up one place and then next door says, “Oh, actually, we could do that”. Suddenly, the domino effect happens. I am all for that—and all for local businesses doing it, by the way, not national businesses.

Dr Joseph Owen: We worked quite a bit in Darlington, which is a historic market town, in 2022. It did a lot of work with Historic England around regeneration that was predicated on the Peases, who gave the library to the town, and there was a lot of narrative around that that people really bought into. On the top-down element, the Darlington Treasury campus was introduced there. When we did research there, we found that people had a sense that they were on the up: there was a feeling of improvement that came from the top-down funding of big infrastructure and capital spending.

However, the top-down element also provided challenges. The yards in Darlington were regenerated but in a very top-down way: they just painted the doors really bright colours. They wanted blue and white stripy awnings. They had stencils of Malala quotes on the wall. Nobody in the local area had a sense of ownership over that at all. In fact, it disrupted their sense of the town centre that they knew, in a way that was not helpful and did not make people feel like they had any attachment, ownership or agency over the place.

You can see the trade-offs here. Sometimes, that top-down stuff gets things in, and there is a sense of economic growth that people feel. At other times, they feel like they have had something they understand taken away from them. The yards have a real industrial history, as we know, which is important to properly foreground, rather than to prettify.

The Chair: Baroness Janke, we have touched on your areas. Is there anything you wish to push on?

Baroness Janke: Yes. Again, I am interested in the interface between the volunteer groups and the other people in the community, whether it is the council, the police, other agencies or the bid teams. Sometimes, it seems to me that there is a difficulty: when people take agency for their particular space—for example, their garden square or the local park—those other people are not necessarily as supportive as they could be. I wonder what your experience of that has been and whether you feel there is a solution. I agree with you that, generally, people need to be in at the start of a project, but sometimes volunteers move in when the council has failed; they take up a project of maintenance, rather than necessarily building a whole new project. Do you have thoughts on that?

Rosie Apperley: I touched earlier on the model that we are trying to build locally in north Islington at the moment, where we are working with our community centres to become nature anchors. The idea of that is partly so we can leverage the contacts of those kinds of organisations, get them in a room with residents and be a bit of a go-between. For a start, if residents understand why something cannot happen, they are often okay with it. Those pathways of communication are often not in existence at all.

I was in a meeting the other day, when the team in charge of depaving in Islington were talking about all the constraints and how they have to decide where they depave according to what is under the ground. We were telling that team to come and tell the residents, because otherwise they will think that the council is just not doing it or is just saying no. If someone can explain all these complicated things that they have to think about, the residents will get it. They are not expecting impossible things.

The idea is building a local community organisation to be that anchor, to bring in those other businesses and local authority organisations and build that connection with residents. “Friends of” groups were mentioned earlier: there is similar infrastructure, where we can bring all those stakeholders together in a local place in a neighbourhood and have an honest conversation—saying, “Actually, no, that tree cannot go in here because of X, Y and Z”. Most of the time, residents will say, “Okay, that makes sense”. It is about having that infrastructure: a local organisation that can hold those relationships and bring all those people together to have that conversation.

Baroness Janke: For example, in my area, a square is being maintained totally by a team of volunteers because the council does very little there, yet the council will let it to a group to run an event there without any consultation, or even any knowledge, of the people who are working in the gardens. There will be a big event, and the plants that the volunteers have raised money to buy and spent their time planting have been vandalised or knocked down by equipment. It is a problem then trying to remotivate people when they are not consulted.

Rosie Apperley: To that question about going beyond funding, some of this is about processes. How can we have a process in place where, if you are looking after a bit of land, you register that in some way and that is logged with the council, and then events cannot go on there without talking to that group?

Similarly, there is a tree pit planting process in Islington. We are trying to keep developing that, because otherwise people plant stuff and it just gets sprayed with pesticides. How can those processes be put in place to allow for this community maintenance not to be destroyed? That needs to happen on a local authority level and across its different departments: the people on the street spraying need to talk to the people sat in an office looking at a spreadsheet. There needs to be that communication.

Baroness Janke: It is easier said than done sometimes, though, is it not?

Rosie Apperley: Absolutely, and the project that we are currently working on—the partnership with Islington Council and the National Trust—is trying to think about how we can do that: having a room full of all the relevant heads of departments at board level in the council, so that they have those cross-departmental conversations that often do not happen. We are in the early days, but this is a real focus in Islington at the moment.

Baroness Janke: The other area that I am interested in is the sustainability of the voluntary groups. My own experience is that you get very good voluntary groups which, as you say, are clear what they are trying to achieve. It may be mums and toddlers wanting play parks or facilities to meet, or sometimes it may be older people who are retired and have particular interests in making an area better. However, once the children go to school and the mums are at work, then suddenly there is a void. Similarly, with the older people’s retired groups, they get older and less able-bodied, and the group whittles away. You are then left with projects that have been initiated but do not have people to sustain them. What do you think about that?

Rosie Apperley: I can answer very quickly. Again, part of the nature anchor model is to have an organisation that has been somewhere for decades that can hold this stuff. As well as all those things, the community in Islington is very transient, and so people come and go. The thinking behind having a local organisation is that it, hopefully, will not go anywhere anytime soon: it can be there in case a group drops off a bit, can step in where needed and can keep that infrastructure going.

There is also the community organising work that we do. Next week, for another local authority I will deliver training in community organising for people who are running local gardening groups. The idea for that is that they have an understanding that part of their running of a gardening group, or volunteering on a small space, is to keep getting new people involved, keep listening to the community and keep engaging more people. Sometimes, these groups can become quite closed and insular. It is about having an organisation behind them to hold them, but also about encouraging them to keep reaching out in their communities, engaging others and getting more people involved.

Baroness Janke: How do you get these organisations behind them? How do you find people? Is it through the statutory bodies such as councils?

Rosie Apperley: We are lucky in that we have 14 community centres in Islington, and I know that that is not the same for lots of other places. It is about identifying organisations that work in a place-based way in a neighbourhood, which may be doing some of this work already, and joining them up.

Baroness Janke: In your experience, have you been successful in having people—volunteers—do a job that you would usually think is the council’s responsibility? There is the busybody element that Shaun mentioned earlier and the idea of “Who are these people telling us what to do? We pay our council tax; it is not for them to be running things around here”. Do you find that to be an issue at all?

Rosie Apperley: There has to be a base level of delivery by the statutory sector. If that is not done effectively, then that will come up. However, people may feel “Actually, the council is looking after this space, but we want to do this thing, so the council does not have to”, and that it is not forced on them because the council does not want to do it or have the funds to do it. That is where we have all said that you need to start from the very beginning. The ideal is that you are creating a new space with the community—they want this space there. Saying to them, “If you want it, look after it” is a lot easier than, “Here is a space. We can’t afford to look after it anymore. Can you do it?” It is about that framing, as well.

Mark Webb: Can I just add to that? Councils should do what only they can do and do it well. I was talking about enabling before, and community groups are really good at getting out of the way of communities. They know how to do that and are good at holding the ring to make sure that these groups are okay, without being overbearing. Local authorities, by their nature, are not so good at that. A good investment of council time and effort would be to consider, if the community that it serves want this thing done, either how to find an existing community group or how to create a community group that would hold the ring on that thing and make sure that it happens.

If they are briefed, talked to and valued in the right way, they will make sure that there is succession planning for people who come and go and that standards are kept up. It will run like any organisation, and you will make sure that you have legacy and longevity in what you created. So it is just about getting out of the way and using community groups to make sure that they can do it. I want to endorse that.

Dr Joseph Owen: I think there is more research to be done on what motivates people to volunteer. We did quite a bit of work in Ledbury and in Dorchester around what makes people, particularly young people, volunteer and about understanding what drives that. It is often a desire for work experience or getting into the workplace to make themselves more attractive in the job market. Those are important things to foreground, as well as the obvious examples of older people who are retired and have more time on their hands. There is something about research there.

From my perspective, part of the project that I am doing for the LGA at the moment is looking at visual arts organisations and the roles that they play in communities. A lot of this is about building trust and having relationships in place. We have to be careful about not overburdening, and the expectations and demands placed on these organisations to do this work. It should not be about trying to make up or compensate for a lack of provision; the point is more about ensuring that they have the tools that they need to do this work. A visual artist, in the example I have given, is not a social worker; they have a particular set of skills, but they cannot compensate for a lack of provision in a place. It is really important to make sure that that balance is struck, and we are doing work on that right now.

The Chair: I think we are probably starting to wrap up, but I have two very quick questions. Dr Owen, you were talking earlier about how top-down intervention in an area was perhaps not the best use of resources and how it was not necessarily welcomed. Are there good examples of where the state has stepped in and done something well, which has gone down very well? Or is it, as Mark described, about being an enabler? Rosie, your experience was about providing guidance.

Is there a risk that, from your point of view, Rosie and Mark, there is an overreliance—maybe we have already crossed that threshold—on good people like yourselves and the work that you do? Actually, there may be a risk that the state, the Secretary of State, the Government or local authorities think, “Actually, we don’t need to do it. You guys are doing it”. Dr Owen, do you have some examples? Give me some good news on when the state does things well.

Dr Joseph Owen: That might have to come in the written evidence. The example I gave earlier comes to mind. As you might imagine, in academia we critique glass and steel a lot, as an approach to doing this work, but our research complicated that. It suggested, actually, that the sense or perception that because things are being built, things are improving—even if the reality is different—is powerful. So there is something that you can do with that perception, as long as it is combined with the grass-roots community work that is co-designed and sustained. They can complement one another. Perhaps I will do a little section in the written evidence with good examples.

Lord Bassam of Brighton: This is relevant to that point. In some places, national government has invested locally by putting, for example, part of the Civil Service there. I am thinking of Blackpool, and Darlington and Grimsby have been mentioned. Can that play a role in triggering better growth locally and better community engagement?

Dr Joseph Owen: Here is the tricky thing. In Darlington—this illustrates it in perhaps a slightly facetious way—you have people coming up from London, for one day a week, on the train. It is pretty quick. They go to the Treasury campus and maybe they spend some money in the newly regenerated yards, which is slightly too expensive for the people who actually live around the area. Then what you have instead is a slightly small visitor economy thing happening, which is not really generating pride, agency, attachment or economic growth in the town. People are spending money, but it is not actually improving the lives of the people.

Northgate is just over the roundabout in Darlington; the people who live there do not even go to the town centre. It is just a short distance over the roundabout, but they do not feel any sense of ownership. It is “not for them”, quote-unquote.

Lord Bassam of Brighton: Decentralising government services and bringing a lot of jobs there surely has an impact.

Dr Joseph Owen: It has an impact, but it is not a panacea. I suppose that that is not the question you were asking either. I am just qualifying that, but it is not without merit.

Mark Webb: For the record, Great Grimsby is the east coast riviera. I would love to bring government departments up there; bring as many as you want and we will house them, no doubt. It is a great place to live and work.

On the idea about whether central or local government will start to hand over things to people, I have to say that there are hundreds of people like me in towns like ours. Some of them need just a bit more encouragement or opportunity to say, “This is what we want”. It does not matter where or what part of the community they come from; there are many courageous leaders or followers who just need to be enabled and to be given the platform or movement to do it.

We have gone quite far in being too paternalistic about what we think the community can and cannot do. There certainly has to be some guidance and guidelines to help people put it on a platform or to be heard. But never underestimate the power of the silent majority of people in our communities—as I said right at the beginning—who are just waiting for an opportunity to step up and step in. We just need to make sure that we give them the power to do that.

The Chair: And the money.

Mark Webb: But you are already spending money on other things. I cannot emphasise enough that it is not about more money. Take Pride in Place, for example. Somebody somewhere said, “Pride in Place is great: £20 million over 10 years will be good for the town”.
