Absolutely, it is, but then—I am not quite sure how—somebody said, “75% of it must be capital and 25% will be revenue”. What was that based on? I do not know where it came from.

Lord Porter of Spalding: That is how the Government spend money. Each department gets allocated some cash to pay for the leccy bill and some cash to put in the electricity metre.

Mark Webb: I understand how capital and revenue work, but I am asking why it is one size fits all for every town. Why not ask them first what they need and then determine how much of that should be capital to make revenue.

Lord Porter of Spalding: Because you are talking about the Treasury; the Treasury never cares about what people need or want.

Mark Webb: I cannot deal with that.

Lord Porter of Spalding: It is what they are getting, because, in their head, it is their money.

The Chair: Let us get Rosie in and then Lord Bailey.

Rosie Apperley: This is outside the remit but, in terms of local organisations and the voluntary sector doing what the state should do, most of our community centres are feeding people and providing warm spaces when they cannot afford to put on the heating. This is an issue. That is something that the voluntary sector is doing in many different areas, but it needs money to keep its own lights on.

Some of that work is rethinking where money goes. I have talked about the work around service level agreements and whether some services and work within the statutory sector could be delivered by the community sector. A lot of it is that mindset shift that I mentioned: think of the voluntary sector and local community organisations as trusted strategic partners and get them involved from the beginning, not just as a stopgap when needed.

Lord Bailey of Paddington: As someone who has been a community worker for more than 35 years—I have to qualify what I am saying—do you not sense the tension here? Every time you bring in a community organisation and give it a statutory role, it just becomes part of the Government. You talked earlier about austerity: well, austerity was not wickedness; austerity was necessary. The public actually voted for it. They were given a choice and they voted for it, because we had so many competing interests and we tried to pay for them all, hence austerity.

Where do you draw the line in giving community services regular income so that they can take on people? Because people make services. A good community organisation could do almost anything because it is about getting good people who will turn their hands to anything. I used to run a charity, and we did everything from family therapy to a football club. We did planting, all kinds of medical programmes, everything. The point is where you would draw the line on that tension about how much they should fund you.

Also, when Lord Porter talks about one size fits all, the one size is not the community; it is the Government. The Government have one mode of behaviour—not always wrong but always criticised. So where is the line? What should community groups not be asked to do and what should they be asked to do? Because I think the community can take more of a load than we are currently asking, but I do accept Rosie’s point; it cannot empty the bins. The Government should be doing that. I accept that. So where would you draw the line, Mark?

Mark Webb: That speaks to the point I made before. I agree that you cannot expect just to fund community groups and keep ploughing money into them in the hope that they will make a difference. But that is not where you start. You start off with what is required and then decide. Sometimes the council or the Government will be exactly the right people to do it, and one size fits all will be exactly the right answer, but many times it is not.

If you look at the need and decide who is best placed, most economically and most effectively, to produce the results that you are looking for, you can stop looking at “Well, it has to be the council first and, if we cannot do it, we will look at to the community groups”. The community groups have to be courageous leaders as well. They have to have a plan and a budget and work to whatever the cards in front of them are, not the cards they wish they had. That is a lesson for us all.

Rosie Apperley: I agree that it can change in places. A specific example is a project that we are working on at the moment in partnership with the council that is about greening. The council is taking up the paving stones, creating the sustainable urban drainage systems and so on. We are doing all the engagement, the light-touch planting and all the getting people involved. It is looking at what the community needs; let us go out and talk to them. What do we want to deliver? Then who is best placed to do that? Then we work together on it and do it together, but have our roles within that. I would not want to draw a line and put one either side.

Dr Joseph Owen: I do not have much more to add, really. These are the guys that are doing that capacity building on the ground. That is the challenge. There are trade-offs to one size fits all. That is the point. You are not going to get what you want from investment in a community if the model does not fit; you are just not going to get the results that you are looking for. They are going to be short term and people will not be invested. The change that you want to see, whether it is improving people’s living standards or their well-being, is not going to happen unless there is that co-design and that capacity building in place.

There is a trade-off to that; it is slower, it takes time and maybe it is more expensive. But then it is more sustainable at the end. That is just the way it works. There are trade-offs the other way as well. You will not get the intervention that you want. I understand that it is a challenge for government to be working within constraints, but these are the recommendations to make this particular sort of work function.

Lord Bailey of Paddington: The recommendations must not be bound by possibility but the outcome will always be so. This is the challenge, is it not? A government cannot commit to 10 years of funding because, even if it is around for 10 years, it does not know what the situation will be then. There is a tension there. Governments give capital because capital is easy to give. I could give you 100 quid today, because I know I have 100 quid. I could promise you 9 quid for the next nine weeks, but I might not have it in eight weeks’ time. That is the tension, but I digress.

The Chair: Please follow up with us in writing, in particular if there is some wider measurable or societal benefit, be it around anti-social behaviour or anything like that, that you can pinpoint for us to demonstrate that there is a benefit.

Mark Webb: We were talking about capital. In my company about 15 years ago, we said to the then local authority that, if it supported a local enterprise growth bid for this social enterprise, it would never have to do business support again because we would make it sustainable. And it has not; for 15 years, we have provided the support by using capital, turning it into revenue and cycling it around that way. That is the kind of discussion you need to have at the beginning to see how this is going to save us in the long term and yet deliver the results that we need, better than the council can. It is possible with a bit of discussion.

Lord Bailey of Paddington: We do need innovation because we have built a sector that just asks for money. It has very little entrepreneurialism and the Government do not have any entrepreneurial bones at all. There is a community-ownership generation model here around particular things: some things just cost money and cannot generate, but other things can. We are not even looking at the difference between the two.

I come from one of the poorest communities in London. Every task we were given, we walked. It was easy to do. But we needed to be asked and being involved generated a muscle. Once we got involved, we really got involved, if you see what I mean. But you needed a council that had the mechanism and, quite frankly, the bravery to do it—the bravery to try and, if it goes wrong, take it back. But it did try.

The Chair: Finally, we have a quickfire round, if I may. If you woke up tomorrow—either from a nightmare or a dream—and you found yourself at 10 Downing Street or as Secretary of State or a council leader, whichever it may be, and you have that role for one day, what one thing would you do? Perhaps it can be more than one thing but, if you can initiate or invoke one change to happen—perhaps if you were sat around this horseshoe like we are—what recommendations would you be making?

Dr Joseph Owen: When you are investing in a physical space, you have to invest in the social infrastructure that is going to sustain it. By that I mean the people, organisations and activities that will make it meaningful. You involve communities and community organisations early doors, exactly as was being said, so that they can change the course of the activity so that it is not predetermined. That is the crucial thing: it is giving communities the flexibility to exercise that genuine power that we are talking about, whether we are talking about revenue and capital funding or what they see as possible. It is not a shopping list in the way that we have talked about, as they actually know what the constraints and limits are, and ask for something that is feasible.

Rosie Apperley: I absolutely agree with all that, and then why not have a paid community organiser in every neighbourhood in the country?

Mark Webb: I would say go to every town in this country and give them 18 months to come up with a plan that is evidentially supported by the community and consulted on by the community. Get them to submit it and say, “These are the things that we want to happen”, and decide then how much money you can allocate from the pot in front of you to make that. But hold the community—not just the council but the council, as well—to account and tell them it is going to be held to account for delivering what it asked for in that plan. Finally, go to Great Grimsby.

The Chair: Thank you very much to all three of you for being with us today. It has been enlightening and fascinating. If there is anything, as I said earlier, that you wish to write to us on, please feel free to do so. It is something that we are increasingly finding interesting. We are keen to hear more about whatever we can do to say to the Government which ideas we think could be easily implemented to help improve the public realm across the country. Thank you very much again.
